research_problem: How, if at all, should evidence from EEG and fMRI command-following paradigms indicating possible awareness in unresponsive patients influence end-of-life decisions?
project_context: A hospital-university team is preparing a mixed-methods ethics and clinical-guidance study on covert consciousness in patients diagnosed with disorders of consciousness. The team includes Dr. Maya Chen, a cognitive neuroscientist; Dr. Samuel Ortiz, an ICU neurologist; and Dr. Eleanor Price, a philosopher of medicine, and they are developing a question that can be investigated with available records and inform family and ethics-committee deliberations.

question_over_time.question: Should EEG or fMRI evidence suggesting awareness in behaviorally unresponsive patients count in end-of-life decisions?
How should positive EEG evidence suggesting covert awareness be used in family conversations and ethics deliberation about withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment when prognosis is poor?

What role should reproducible positive EEG command-following evidence of possible covert awareness play in later deliberations about withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment for behaviorally unresponsive patients with an otherwise poor neurological prognosis?

drivers_of_change.driver: Available records and clinical practice make EEG feasible and fMRI rare; the records support studying deliberation and communication rather than whether a test directly caused a withdrawal decision. The team also recognizes that isolated negative findings cannot rule out awareness.

The protocol requires a defensible definition of informative positive evidence and a decision stage less distorted by acute sedation and metabolic confounders, so it specifies reproducible or convergent positive EEG evidence and later prognostic withdrawal deliberations.

ground_truth.what_stayed_constant: The project consistently concerns behaviorally unresponsive patients who may have covert awareness, the uncertainty and limitations of command-following neurodiagnostic evidence, and the ethical-clinical question of how that evidence should inform end-of-life decisions without becoming a sole determinant of withdrawal.

meetings.label: Meeting 1 — March 3, 2027

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Cognitive neuroscientist with 11 years of experience designing and analyzing EEG and fMRI studies of consciousness, including mental-imagery and auditory command-following paradigms in patients with disorders of consciousness. She leads protocol implementation and signal-quality review for a hospital-university neuroimaging program, working with preprocessing pipelines, single-subject statistical inference, artifact detection, and bedside-compatible EEG. Her work has included patients whose motor output is absent or inconsistent, and she routinely collaborates with speech-language, rehabilitation, and critical-care teams.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats command-following signals as indirect, technically mediated evidence: a reproducible task-contingent neural response can support an inference that a patient may have understood and intentionally followed a command despite absent behavior. She emphasizes that nonresponse is not straightforward evidence of no awareness, because movement, sedatives, fluctuating arousal, hearing or language limitations, scanner tolerance, and the demands of a particular task can all yield false negatives. She is eager to clarify what the tests can and cannot establish, while recognizing that clinical and ethical implications must be developed with the other disciplines.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Eleanor Price
speakers.background: PhD candidate in philosophy of medicine in her sixth year, with prior training in bioethics and qualitative interview methods. Her dissertation examines evidentiary thresholds, uncertainty, and surrogate decision-making in disorders of consciousness. She has conducted interviews with clinicians, family members, and ethics consultants about how diagnostic labels and technologically generated findings shape interpretations of patient interests, and she is experienced in conceptual analysis of prognosis, autonomy, welfare, and moral status.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Price insists on separating two questions that are often run together: whether a finding warrants an inference that the patient is aware, and what moral or clinical significance that awareness should have for a treatment decision. Evidence of awareness may alter beliefs about experience, communication potential, prognosis, or the appropriateness of further assessment, but none of those consequences follows automatically. She focuses on how uncertainty should be represented in deliberation and how patient values and family interpretations mediate the relevance of evidence.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
speakers.background: ICU neurologist with 17 years of post-residency practice at a tertiary academic medical center. He directs a neurocritical-care service and regularly evaluates patients with acute brain injury, prolonged unresponsiveness, and disorders of consciousness. His practice includes serial standardized bedside examinations, neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest and traumatic brain injury, family conferences, palliative-care consultation, and participation in hospital ethics reviews concerning withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. He uses EEG, structural and functional imaging, and longitudinal clinical data as parts of—not substitutes for—clinical judgment.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Ortiz approaches withdrawal-of-life-sustaining-treatment deliberations as longitudinal, patient-specific decisions rather than reactions to a single diagnostic result. In the ICU, prognosis is assembled from etiology, timing, sedation and metabolic confounders, serial neurologic examination, electrophysiology and imaging where appropriate, trajectory, and the patient’s known values as understood by surrogates. He sees a possible covert-consciousness finding as potentially important information that may prompt reassessment or a more careful conversation, but he resists treating any isolated test as determinative of prognosis or of what treatment a patient would have wanted.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Hi, both. It’s oddly bright here after all that rain. Feels a little unfair for a March Monday. I thought today we could get clear on the clinical decision we actually want to study. Not whether these signals prove awareness in some broad sense, but where an uncertain positive result might change what happens in a real family or ethics conversation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: The rain at least kept the unit mercifully quiet this weekend. Clinically, I'd resist putting this at a single decision. Withdrawal is usually a series of conversations, but we could ask how a positive, uncertain command-following result gets taken up alongside the serial exam, etiology, and trajectory, and whether it changes the deliberation rather than assuming it should change the outcome...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm, the deliberation piece.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I think that keeps us from smuggling in the conclusion that a signal of possible awareness has one fixed implication. In interviews, "there may be awareness" has meant hope to one family and possible suffering to another, so I'd be interested in how that uncertainty is actually presented—represented in the conversation, not just whether the result appears in the chart.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And the chart may say "EEG positive" without preserving what the family was actually told about it. Eleanor, do you have a sense of wording that lets people hear, hear "this is meaningful evidence of command-following" without having them infer that we know prognosis or what the patient is experiencing? Because technically, those are really separate leaps.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I'd probably avoid one explanatory phrase, because it invites exactly those further inferences. Something like, “This test provides limited evidence that your relative may have understood and responded to an instruction at that time. It does not, on its own, tell us how much they are experiencing, whether they can communicate reliably, or what recovery is likely.” But we should ask families how that lands. I was going to say “limited” can sound- it can sound either dismissive or much more certain than we intend.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That feels much closer to what the signal can bear. A positive result is evidence tied to that time and that task. It says something happened under those conditions, not that we have a stable channel to the person. Sam, in the actual conversations, what kind of finding makes the team pause, repeat an assessment, or revisit the prognosis, even if nobody treats it as dispositive?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: What makes me slow down isn’t really one category of test result. It’s more a discordance, a positive command-following paradigm in someone whose motor output is absent or wildly inconsistent, especially when the bedside exam has been clouded by sedation, seizures, or metabolic issues. I’d repeat the standardized exam off confounders if we can, review the EEG background and reactivity, and ask whether the trajectory and structural injury actually, uh, cohere. A signal alone doesn’t reverse a grim prognosis, but it can make premature closure much harder to justify.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That discordance may be the most useful anchor for the records work. Not positive test equals changed decision, but what the team did when the signal didn't fit the exam. I'd want to know whether we can reconstruct the confounders at the time of testing, especially sedation, but also hearing, language, and whether the patient could tolerate the task, because otherwise a negative comparison group- it gets pretty slippery.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Hm, yes, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: And the timing matters too, frankly. A medication administration record can tell us what was ordered, but not always whether the patient was still clinically sedated when the paradigm ran. Renal failure, prolonged infusions, all of that matters. Before we make discordance the cohort definition, I need to see if we can reliably line up the test time, confounders, serial exams, and the family conference notes across the ICU and rehab records, because otherwise...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, and it may be different by modality: fMRI logs usually give us a cleaner acquisition time, while bedside EEG can be more granular but the task notes are often uneven. Before we define the cohort, could we do a small chart audit—say, ten or fifteen cases—to see whether that alignment is actually recoverable?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: I think that’s the right first move. I’d want the audit to include cases where the apparent bedside trajectory later changed, because the formal diagnostic label may look stable while the daily examinations were anything but. And we should see whether the conference documentation tells us who was present and whether the result was discussed before or after a limitation-of-treatment decision. Otherwise, we’ll- otherwise we’ll mistake chronology for influence.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yes—and for the audit, I’d separate the test date, the result-review date, and the conference date. Otherwise, a result can look like it informed a limitation decision when it was really reported afterward. I’m also wondering if we should include the raw task documentation as an audit field. “EEG positive” can conceal whether there was a repeatable command-linked effect or just preserved auditory processing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Exactly. We need to distinguish a reproducible, appropriately controlled command-following effect from an auditory or attentional response, because clinically those would trigger pretty different levels of reassessment. And I'd add whether the interpreting clinician documented uncertainty or, um, alternative explanations, because the raw trace may be available, but the charted interpretation is what the treating team and family were actually acting on.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d make those separate fields instead of one “positive” box. The task and control condition, whether the effect repeated, and then the clinician’s own wording on confidence or caveat. The two bedside EEG cases we saw recently are a good reminder. Both had intact auditory responses, but only one had a repeatable command-linked pattern, and that distinction could just disappear in a summary note, so—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: That distinction matters ethically too, because families may hear both labels as just, “they’re in there.” I’d include a separate field for what was communicated to the family, if the notes permit it, and whether the uncertainty about repeatability and alternative explanations was conveyed, rather than just the headline result.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: I’d want us to code not just whether uncertainty was stated, but what happened after that. Was there a repeat examination, a delay in a limitation decision, an ethics or palliative-care consult, or nothing discernible? That gets us closer to clinical uptake without pretending the chart can tell us exactly why a family decided as it did.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And “nothing discernible” matters too. It may mean the result never reached the conference, not that it was considered and discounted. Could we also code whether a repeat paradigm was technically feasible and whether it was actually attempted? A one-off positive and a failed or unavailable repeat are very different evidential situations, but I’m not sure how often we’ll be able to see that in these records.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: That’s worth separating in the audit. Unavailable or infeasible is not the same as an attempted repeat that fails to replicate. And if a repeat was not pursued, the notes may sometimes tell us whether that was understood as a technical constraint, a judgment that it would not alter care, or simply, simply never considered. Those are ethically rather different silences.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That gives us a useful feasibility distinction, rather than treating missing repeats as negative evidence. For the audit, I’d also flag whether the original task itself was compromised by hearing barriers, language mismatch, arousal, excessive movement. I was going to say a nonrepeat- under those conditions, it really doesn’t mean the first signal was spurious. Then we can see what the notes actually let us say before we build the larger question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Right, and that’s easy to miss.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: The audit should also capture the clinical state on the day, not just the formal diagnosis. Was the exam fluctuating, was there any purposeful-looking behavior, and what confounders remained? Otherwise, we may call something a conflict between modalities when really the patient's responsiveness was changing hour to hour.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Otherwise we risk calling ordinary fluctuation a mismatch. For the audit, I think we should timestamp the closest standardized exam and the relevant sedation or metabolic context. Rather than trying to collapse the whole day into one clinical label, we can see whether the signal was genuinely surprising in context. I’ll check what the EEG and fMRI archives actually preserve for that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Good. And I’d include what happened with each ambiguity, whether a later bedside finding resolved it, repeat testing did, or it just carried forward into the conference. If the ten or fifteen charts can’t give us that chronology across the ICU-to-rehab boundary, then we should narrow the study rather than—rather than manufacture a causal story from the order of the notes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: If the chronology is thin, I’d rather describe the study as mapping how uncertainty was documented and taken up than claim it changed a decision. And for the audit, we should also note when the record contains the family’s own interpretation at all, because the same clinical sequence can mean quite different things depending on what they took possible awareness to mean.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, I think that’s key.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Given the time, I think the pilot should tell us whether we can preserve that distinction without overreading it. What the family was told, what they appeared to understand, and then the subsequent clinical response—not, I was going to say, not an inferred causal effect on withdrawal. If those pieces are mostly absent, that itself sets the limit of the records question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there, we’re at time. I’ll follow up by email about the small chart review, sorry, audit, and thank you both. This was really helpful.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Thanks, Maya. Take care, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Morning. It’s oddly bright here after the rain. Better than trying to get across campus in it, I guess. I’ve got a family conference later this morning, so I was hoping we could use this time to see whether the charts actually support the question we’ve been circling. The chronology around EEG findings, the conversations, and what happened after. I did a first pass through the available cases, and there are some promising things, but fMRI is a pretty important limitation because...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Mm, okay.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The fMRI limitation is important, especially if all we can recover is the scan date and not the exact clinical state around it. Before we decide how much weight to put on it, Sam, what do the charts usually retain for the EEG indication and bedside conditions? Could we tell whether it was done in anything like a stable examination window? I was going to ask about the- whether we can actually place it in a stable exam window.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: It’s inconsistent. The EEG order usually gives an indication, seizure concern, unexplained encephalopathy, sometimes prognostication, and the report has the recording conditions. But the actual bedside state is often only recoverable by triangulating the nursing flowsheets and the daily exam. You’re looking at sedative infusions, recent paralytic, temperature, metabolic issues. A stable window is plausible in some cases, but not demonstrable in all. And these are routine clinical EEGs, not generally command-following paradigms, so Maya, I need your view on what in the preserved report would distinguish a task-linked signal from- I lost my thread there. From a nonspecific change.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: On a routine EEG report, that's probably not enough. We'd need a record that they used a specific instruction and a time-locked analysis. Otherwise, a change in background activity or an auditory evoked response isn't command-following. I need to check what the older archive actually retains, raw EEG, montage details, and technologist notes, because without those, we may have to treat EEG as documentation of clinical interpretation rather than re-adjudicating the signal independently.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Exactly. If we can't establish that a task was given and the response was time-locked to it, then clinically we shouldn't call the EEG evidence of covert command-following at all. For the audit, I think we should code that distinction explicitly. Documented task-linked finding, nonspecific EEG finding that was later interpreted optimistically, and indeterminate because the underlying materials are absent. Otherwise, we'll accidentally manufacture a signal from ordinary monitoring.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That three-way coding is the right safeguard. For a documented task-linked finding, I'd want the task itself, some indication of when it happened, and whether it was repeated or had any signal-quality caveat, because an isolated positive isn't all the same thing either. I'm a little worried the technologist notes may be the only place interruptions or arousal shifts show up.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: And clinically, those interruptions matter a great deal. If the technologist note says the patient was drifting off, being suctioned, or had a clear arousal change during the task, that's not just a minor technical footnote. It changes what we can say the response meant. For the audit, I'd keep a separate field for whether the source material supports interpretation at all, rather than, rather than collapsing that into positive versus negative.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: That source-support field matters ethically too, I think, because a chart can later carry forward "EEG suggests awareness" without preserving what, um, what warranted that phrase. Maya, once you've seen the archive, what wording would you regard as fair for a genuinely task-contingent response, something that doesn't quietly turn it into a claim about broad awareness or prognosis?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'd say, "This task produced a reproducible brain response consistent with following the instruction," if that's what the record supports. And then I'd explicitly add that it's a possible sign of preserved awareness, not a prediction of recovery. And for negatives, I think the paired wording has to be there too. A single negative EEG or fMRI task doesn't show absence of awareness. It may just reflect drowsiness, hearing, attention, language, or- sorry, task mismatch.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: And that is probably the language we need to trace in the family notes too, whether the limitation travels with the positive finding or whether it gets compressed into, um, "there is awareness." Eleanor, if a note says uncertainty was discussed but never says how the surrogate weighed it, what do you think we can responsibly claim about the deliberation?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: We can claim only that the chart documents the clinicians' account of the deliberation, not the surrogate's actual reasoning or that the finding influenced the decision. "Uncertainty discussed" is especially thin. It may mean the caveat was said aloud, but not whether it was understood, or whether the family took it as reassurance, warning, or something else. I'd code that as uptake not assessable rather than infer a neutral effect, because we just don't know—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Uptake not assessable seems exactly right, rather than making any claim about influence. I found several conference notes entered days later that bundle multiple conversations, so even the order of the result, the discussion, and the decision may be, um, irretrievable in some cases. We should probably make chronology confidence its own variable and not pretend the note timestamp is the encounter time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I’d separate chronology confidence from communication quality. A note written late may still preserve the clinician’s framing, but it’s much weaker evidence that the finding entered the family’s reasoning before a decision. Sam, do ethics-consult notes give us a more contemporaneous- a more timely account in enough of these cases, or are they too uneven across ICU and rehab to use as a common source?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: It’s uneven, I’m afraid. When ethics is involved, their notes can be quite useful and often more explicit about the competing prognostic uncertainties and the values question. But consultation itself is selective, so it can’t be our common source or treated as evidence that a case was especially contested. I’d abstract it as an ancillary, higher-detail source, then see in the pilot how often it actually helps resolve those bundled conference notes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d want to see whether those ancillary notes ever preserve the actual wording of the result. Whether it stayed “possible sign” with the task limits attached, or whether it had already become a broader statement about awareness. And if ethics notes help only in a few cases, that’s still useful for the pilot, but it’s not something we can use to fill gaps in the ordinary conference record.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s helpful.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: I think the pilot has to show us not just whether a phrase appears, but whether its evidentiary qualifiers, qualifiers survive across neurology, ethics, and family-conference documentation. And before we decide this can become a larger cohort, I still need to confirm the eligible case count and whether the rehabilitation record links cleanly enough to the ICU chart. Otherwise, we may be describing two disconnected pieces of a trajectory.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And the linkage question affects the signal side too. If a later rehab note says the patient was more alert or followed something behaviorally, we shouldn’t use that to retroactively validate an ambiguous ICU EEG. Could we keep those as later clinical observations, with their own dates, rather than treating the whole trajectory as one continuous evidentiary, I mean, clinical record?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Later behavioral observations are clinically important, but they’re not- we can’t use them as post hoc ground truth for an equivocal ICU recording. We should date them separately and record the changes in between, like sedation clearance, complications, and rehabilitation exposure, instead of treating them as validation. That also keeps the longitudinal picture honest when we ask what information was available at the time of a goals-of-care conversation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: For the ethics question, I think that temporal discipline is crucial. We should ask what this result could reasonably have contributed to deliberation at that moment, not let later improvement, or decline, settle what it meant then. Otherwise we end up treating the chart as though everyone, everyone had hindsight.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm-hm, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: The abstraction should preserve the clinical information that was available at each conference, including what was uncertain and which confounders were still active, instead of letting the eventual outcome rewrite it. If the pilot gives us enough cleanly dated cases, that feels like a defensible study. If not, we narrow it to how the finding and its caveats moved through the record.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Mm, I think so.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah—keeping it to the record trail if chronology fails feels right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: All right, I think we should leave it there. I’ll follow up by email once I’ve checked the linkage and the final eligible count. Thanks, both. This was really helpful.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Thanks, Sam. Good luck with the conference later.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Bye, both—talk soon.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Cognitive neuroscientist with 11 years of experience designing and analyzing EEG and fMRI studies of consciousness, including mental-imagery and auditory command-following paradigms in patients with disorders of consciousness. She leads protocol implementation and signal-quality review for a hospital-university neuroimaging program, working with preprocessing pipelines, single-subject statistical inference, artifact detection, and bedside-compatible EEG. Her work has included patients whose motor output is absent or inconsistent, and she routinely collaborates with speech-language, rehabilitation, and critical-care teams.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen treats command-following signals as indirect, technically mediated evidence: a reproducible task-contingent neural response can support an inference that a patient may have understood and intentionally followed a command despite absent behavior. She emphasizes that nonresponse is not straightforward evidence of no awareness, because movement, sedatives, fluctuating arousal, hearing or language limitations, scanner tolerance, and the demands of a particular task can all yield false negatives. She is eager to clarify what the tests can and cannot establish, while recognizing that clinical and ethical implications must be developed with the other disciplines.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Eleanor Price
speakers.background: PhD candidate in philosophy of medicine in her sixth year, with prior training in bioethics and qualitative interview methods. Her dissertation examines evidentiary thresholds, uncertainty, and surrogate decision-making in disorders of consciousness. She has conducted interviews with clinicians, family members, and ethics consultants about how diagnostic labels and technologically generated findings shape interpretations of patient interests, and she is experienced in conceptual analysis of prognosis, autonomy, welfare, and moral status.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Price insists on separating two questions that are often run together: whether a finding warrants an inference that the patient is aware, and what moral or clinical significance that awareness should have for a treatment decision. Evidence of awareness may alter beliefs about experience, communication potential, prognosis, or the appropriateness of further assessment, but none of those consequences follows automatically. She focuses on how uncertainty should be represented in deliberation and how patient values and family interpretations mediate the relevance of evidence.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
speakers.background: ICU neurologist with 17 years of post-residency practice at a tertiary academic medical center. He directs a neurocritical-care service and regularly evaluates patients with acute brain injury, prolonged unresponsiveness, and disorders of consciousness. His practice includes serial standardized bedside examinations, neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest and traumatic brain injury, family conferences, palliative-care consultation, and participation in hospital ethics reviews concerning withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment. He uses EEG, structural and functional imaging, and longitudinal clinical data as parts of—not substitutes for—clinical judgment.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Ortiz approaches withdrawal-of-life-sustaining-treatment deliberations as longitudinal, patient-specific decisions rather than reactions to a single diagnostic result. In the ICU, prognosis is assembled from etiology, timing, sedation and metabolic confounders, serial neurologic examination, electrophysiology and imaging where appropriate, trajectory, and the patient’s known values as understood by surrogates. He sees a possible covert-consciousness finding as potentially important information that may prompt reassessment or a more careful conversation, but he resists treating any isolated test as determinative of prognosis or of what treatment a patient would have wanted.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

meetings.meeting_context:
A hospital-university team is preparing a mixed-methods ethics and clinical-guidance study on covert consciousness in patients diagnosed with disorders of consciousness. The team includes Dr. Maya Chen, a cognitive neuroscientist; Dr. Samuel Ortiz, an ICU neurologist; and Dr. Eleanor Price, a philosopher of medicine, and they are developing a question that can be investigated with available records and inform family and ethics-committee deliberations.

Meeting 3 — April 14, 2027. Protocol-finalization meeting to define the study question, inclusion criteria, and the decision context the resulting guidance will address.

What the team remembers from earlier meetings:
Meeting 1 — March 3, 2027: The group reframed the study around how uncertain command-following findings are documented, communicated, and taken up in clinical and family deliberations, rather than whether they determine withdrawal decisions or prove awareness broadly. The immediate plan is a 10–15 case chart audit before defining a larger cohort, testing whether records can reliably align test, result-review, and family-conference dates across ICU and rehabilitation care. Maya will follow up on the audit and check what EEG and fMRI archives preserve; the audit will distinguish task features, repeatability, clinician caveats, timing, bedside state, confounders, repeat-test feasibility, and subsequent clinical actions. The research question remains focused on discordance between a possible command-following signal and the clinical examination, including how uncertainty and alternative explanations were conveyed to families and what happened afterward. Open issues are whether sedation and other confounders, chronology, family interpretations, and communication details can be recovered well enough from records; if not, the study will be narrowed to mapping documentation and clinical uptake rather than claiming causal influence on decisions.
Meeting 2 — March 24, 2027: The study will examine how potentially task-linked EEG/fMRI findings, their caveats, and subsequent communication appear in the record around goals-of-care discussions, while preserving what was knowable at each point rather than using later outcomes as validation. EEG findings will be coded as documented task-linked, nonspecific later interpreted optimistically, or indeterminate, with separate fields for source support, interruptions/confounders, chronology confidence, and whether surrogate uptake is assessable. Maya will check what the older EEG archive retains, including raw data, montage details, and technologist notes, and advise on defensible wording for task-contingent findings. Sam will confirm the eligible case count and ICU–rehabilitation linkage, abstract ethics notes only as ancillary sources, and email the group with the results. If the pilot yields enough cleanly dated linked cases, the project can study deliberation over time; otherwise it will narrow to tracing how findings and qualifiers moved through the record. Open issues are the limited and inconsistent fMRI/EEG source materials, uncertain chronology in delayed bundled notes, uneven ethics documentation, and whether rehabilitation records link cleanly enough to ICU charts.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Morning. It is, mercifully, not raining here for once, although the unit was already full before seven, so I may be a little behind the curve. Um, for today, I think we need to land on a cohort definition that captures the actual later deliberation, not the first ICU conversation when half the exam may still be, uh, confounded, and decide whether the pilot records can really support that chronology.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Mm, that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Morning. I agree, especially since an early bedside EEG can be hard to interpret when sedation or arousal is moving around. Sam, do these charts usually give us enough clearly dated medication and metabolic context to say whether a task run was, was interpretable? And can we actually separate the later prognostic conversations from the bundled notes?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Usually there’s enough to identify exposure, yes, but not enough to certify an unconfounded exam from a medication list alone. I’d code the actual documented state—sedation held or ongoing, organ failure, seizures, metabolic derangement—and treat missingness as meaningful. For the later conferences, the copied-forward notes are the real- what we need is an encounter anchor, rather than accepting the signature date.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For the EEG side, could we make the interpretability field separate from the result itself? So a note saying “consistent with command following” isn’t treated the same when we have task timing, artifact notes, and a documented bedside state, versus when we only have that one sentence in a consult note.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Exactly. I’d make that a separate axis, and I wouldn’t let a consult’s conclusion backfill the evidentiary fields. Maya, on the source data, what would you regard as enough to call an EEG effect reproducible rather than a one-off analytic artifact? Does a repeat, repeat task run do the same work as convergent support from fMRI, or are those really answering different questions?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: They’re related, but they’re not interchangeable. A repeat run of the same well-specified task, with the same task-contingent pattern and usable artifact documentation, is the cleanest evidence that it wasn’t a one-off. A convergent fMRI result can- it can strengthen the overall inference, but it has its own timing and feasibility problems. I’d code both separately rather than let either one automatically substitute for the other.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Even with repeatability or convergence, we should keep the caveat that this supports a task-contingent inference. It isn't proof of a particular conscious experience or prognosis. Maya, would you be comfortable spelling out what residual alternatives remain in that highest-evidence category, so the later deliberation coding doesn't quietly turn it into "the patient is aware"?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Even in that category, we could still have task misunderstanding, residual artifact or analysis error, fluctuating attention, and limits in what the task itself samples. It doesn't tell us how stable awareness is or what the patient would want. I'd phrase it as "reproducible evidence compatible with intentional command following," and then keep track of whether it was repeated, convergent, and interpretable at the time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Good. Then the cohort should not be "positive test" cases in any broad sense. It should be patients who are still behaviorally unresponsive after the major acute confounders were addressed, with an otherwise poor prognosis under active consideration and an actual later goals-of-care deliberation. Eleanor, when that finding, that finding enters the room, what does it mean operationally to say it changes safeguards or reasons rather than the outcome? What language could a clinician actually put in a conference note?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I think it would be something like, this finding doesn't resolve prognosis or establish the patient's treatment preferences, but it raises enough uncertainty about awareness that we should review confounders, consider whether reassessment is feasible, and revisit the patient's known values before we treat prognosis as settled. For the audit, though, I'd code those as distinct elements. Otherwise, a note can sound careful without ever actually recording, say, a time-limited reassessment discussion.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: And I think that distinction is the whole value of the audit. In the charts, I’m worried we’ll find language like “continue to observe” without any indication whether that was a response to the signal, a family request, or just a new attending’s framing. So we should code the safeguard explicitly, and separately code whether the note attributes it to the test— to the signal at all.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And on the signal side, I think we should guard against a parallel ambiguity. The cohort trigger can't be just any EEG abnormality. Diffuse slowing, reactivity, or an odd waveform isn't command following. I'd require a documented task-linked signature, and then distinguish a one-off from a reproducible positive—reproducible positive EEG command-following signature, with repeat runs ideally and the source details there to support it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Right, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: I’d keep the one-off cases in if the documentation says task-linked, because clinically those are exactly the awkward findings that can enter a family conversation even though they’re technically weak. But we need a separate evidentiary tier. We can’t let “possible signal” collapse into the reproducible category. Then we should ask whether either tier was actually available before the conference encounter, instead of reconstructing it later from a consult note.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: And for the deliberation part, I’d distinguish “the finding was disclosed” from “the finding was taken up.” A conference note may only show the first. We should probably reserve any claim about surrogate uptake for cases where the family’s question, interpretation, or stated reason is actually, actually documented, rather than infer it from continued treatment afterward.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Continued treatment is an outcome, not evidence of why anybody chose it. For the pilot, I think we need an attribution field with pretty unforgiving categories. Explicitly linked to the finding, explicitly linked to another reason, competing explanations documented, or, um, not ascertainable. That late-consult case I mentioned is probably in that last category unless the actual encounter note gives us more than the copied-forward language.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The timing field matters for us too. A finding only counts as available for that deliberation if the task and its interpretation were documented before the anchored conference, not just summarized afterward. I’m seeing that exact problem in the pilot, two charts both say “consistent with command following,” but one has two runs and artifact notes, and the other is just a later consult- it’s just a later consult sentence.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: For eligibility, I want a hard temporal rule. The task-linked result or its documented interpretation has to come before the anchored goals-of-care encounter. And before we lock that in, I still need to verify the actual linked-case count. Particularly whether the rehab encounters and the ICU chart- whether they give us enough clean anchors, rather than creating a cohort on paper that we can't reconstruct.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I think that hard rule is right, as long as we also retain a category for findings documented after the encounter but described as having been discussed. I lost my thread there. It’s a chronology problem, not evidence that they informed the decision. Otherwise we may mistake a retrospective narrative for what the family and clinicians could actually have known then.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Keep it, but flag it as retrospective chronology rather than letting it satisfy the exposure rule. For the pilot, the practical question is whether we can anchor enough conferences to an actual encounter, like a same-day palliative note, orders, bedside documentation, something, because otherwise even a beautifully categorized signal has nowhere reliable to sit in the deliberation timeline and...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Mm. And if we can't anchor the encounter, I'd be reluctant to code more than documentation flow. That the result and a goals-of-care note both exist, not that one informed the other. Could the pilot use a minimum anchor, say an encounter note plus either contemporaneous orders or a same-day note from another service, before we call the chronology usable—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: I think that's a sensible minimum, with one caveat. Orders may reflect a decision made hours earlier, so I wouldn't require them if we have two independently authored, contemporaneous clinical notes that identify the encounter. The key is that we can place the conversation in time without using a copied-forward, um, summary as the anchor. Otherwise, yes, we stop at documentation flow.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Yeah, that seems important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: Mm. On that minimum anchor, I'd add that the conference note has to have some substantive account of the discussion, not just "family updated." Otherwise, we may be able to place the encounter in time, but we still- we still have no basis for saying how uncertainty, or the finding, was communicated.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: The usable-deliberation subset needs both, a defensible encounter anchor and substantive content. We need to know what prognosis was discussed, whether the task finding and its limits were communicated, and whether any reassessment or time-limited observation was considered. If all we have is “family updated,” that goes in the record inventory, but it can't- we can't use it to infer uptake or safeguards.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: I'd make that substantive-content threshold quite literal in the codebook. Not just whether the finding appears, but whether its uncertainty and limits are represented along with prognosis, reassessment, and the patient's values. If those are absent, we can say the record documents disclosure, perhaps, but not ethically adequate deliberation, or even what the family was being asked to consider— to weigh.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Given the hard stop, I think that's enough to finalize the pilot threshold. A task-linked finding before a substantively documented, anchored later deliberation, and otherwise we describe documentation flow only. I'll verify the linked-case count and those encounter dates—encounter anchors—before we pretend the larger cohort is feasible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Eleanor Price
transcript.text: All right, I think we can let everyone go a few minutes early. Thanks, both, this was really helpful, and we’ll pick it up once Sam has had a look at those anchors.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Samuel Ortiz
transcript.text: Great. Take care, both.

ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style with mostly short to medium turns, though formal presentation segments contain long, dense monologues. Early and late discussion is highly conversational, with frequent greetings, side chatter, repetitions, and occasional loose overlap or abrupt handoffs. Speakers use many fillers and repairs—“um,” “yeah,” “okay,” “sort of,” “you know,” repeated starts, and self-corrections—especially when asking questions or thinking aloud. The tone is informal and encouraging even in technical discussion; participants praise talks before questioning them and frame challenges as curiosity (“I’m just curious,” “naive question,” “do you think,” “have you looked at…”). Questions are often multipart, exploratory, and prefaced with hedges or brief compliments. Disagreement is rare and indirect; speakers qualify claims, acknowledge uncertainty, and treat alternatives as open possibilities. Participants build on prior remarks by restating a point, linking it to related work, or extending it into a possible collaboration, while the host uses concise transitions and reminders to keep the session moving.

Meeting style for this meeting (one_voice_leads): One person (often the most senior) talks for much of the meeting in long turns. Others come in with short questions or one-line agreement. A quieter person speaks rarely and usually only when asked directly or after a pause.
